title: Overview: the big ideas
summary: The chapter's key concepts and how its sections fit together.

blocks.md: Welcome to **Test-Time Compute** (Vol III). This overview gives you the chapter's big ideas before the section-by-section lessons. Read the claims once, flip the flashcards, then take the warm-up quiz: it is fine to miss questions here, the lessons that follow fill the gaps.

An agent that deliberates before acting pays latency and money for a better chance of success, whether it spends them on a longer derivation, more candidate patches, an extra check, or another model call. Each purchase answers a different question. More tokens re-examine what the prompt already holds, more candidates raise the chance that a good one sits somewhere in the pool, and only an executed check adds a fact the model did not have.

rows: **Allocation axes**
Depth, breadth, and feedback can spend the same output ceiling yet differ in critical path, retained KV state, and bill, and only feedback adds information the prompt and weights lack.
**Budgeted deliberation**
Test-time compute is a per-decision allowance that sets the attempt cost in C_eff, so it pays only when it raises acceptance faster than cost, and difficulty should route the budget.
**Coverage is not selection**

pass@k = 1-(1-p)^k caps any selector that returns an unchanged pool member, while realized accuracy is set by the selector, so coverage near 98 percent can coexist with a vote that plateaus near half.
**Ranking is not acceptance**
Voting and learned ranking both return the best failure from a defective pool, so only selection by a check the candidate cannot modify justifies returning a candidate instead of abstaining.
**Verifier precision**

The precision of a passing verdict depends on the valid-candidate base rate and the check's error rates, not on pool size, so a larger pool raises both the chance of a selection and the chance of a false pass.
**Selection pressure**
Argmax over N noisy scores selects positive error growing like sigma*sqrt(2 ln N) and crowns any exploit present in the pool, so check accuracy must be re-measured on selected candidates.
**Step-level evidence**

Outcome checks execute a finished candidate while reward models only predict quality, and step checks prune failing branches early at the cost of false rejections and scorer input that grows quadratically without prefix reuse.
**Revisable candidate plans**
Recording a candidate as a dependency graph of artifacts with evidence provenance lets a refuting observation invalidate exactly its descendants while retained branches keep their support.
**Search tree pruning**
A step check that rejects a fraction r of b children gives an effective branching factor b(1-r), so a tree stays finite on its own only when r > 1-1/b and otherwise needs hard caps.
**Search accounting**
A search tracks money, non-interchangeable work, wall time, and peak live state in separate accounts and reserves each request's maximum charge before dispatch, releasing it only on settlement.
**Stopping precedence**
Before admitting more work, apply hard ceilings, then satisficing, then marginal stopping, and an exhausted budget returns unresolved or escalates rather than lowering the acceptance threshold.
**Deliberation operating point**
A deliberation policy's operating point is chosen on the cost-acceptance-deadline frontier, with false acceptance, abstention, and deadline exhaustion reported separately.
